title: Medicare 101 for New Jerseyans turning 65
dek: The parts, the deadlines, the 2026 costs and the penalties that last a lifetime. Here is how to get Medicare right the first time, with a month-by-month plan and free help from SHIP.
keyFacts: Your Initial Enrollment Period lasts 7 months, centered on your 65th birthday month.
2026 Part B premium: $202.90 a month. Part B deductible: $283.
Part B late penalty: 10% for each full 12 months you could have enrolled but did not, usually for life.
Working past 65? If your employer has 20 or more employees, you can usually delay Part B without penalty.
Free, unbiased Medicare counseling in NJ: SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.
body:
Turning 65 in New Jersey brings a pile of mail. Insurance agents call. TV ads promise extra benefits. Under all that noise sits a simple set of rules. Learn them once and you can make a calm, confident choice.

This guide covers the four parts of Medicare, when to sign up, what to do if you are still working, how to avoid penalties and what Medicare costs in 2026. It ends with a month-by-month timeline and a word about New Jersey's free counseling program.

What are the four parts of Medicare?

Medicare is federal health insurance for people 65 and older, and for some younger people with disabilities. It comes in pieces, called parts.

  • Part A (hospital insurance) covers inpatient hospital stays, some skilled nursing facility care after a hospital stay, hospice and some home health care. Most people pay no premium for Part A because they or a spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes for about 10 years (40 quarters).
  • Part B (medical insurance) covers doctor visits, outpatient care, lab work, scans, durable medical equipment and many preventive services. Almost everyone pays a monthly premium.
  • Part C (Medicare Advantage) is an all-in-one alternative run by private insurers approved by Medicare. It bundles Parts A and B, and usually Part D, often with a network of doctors and hospitals.
  • Part D (prescription drug coverage) is sold by private plans. You can buy a stand-alone Part D plan alongside Original Medicare, or get drug coverage inside a Medicare Advantage plan.

"Original Medicare" means Parts A and B together. Many people on Original Medicare add a Medicare Supplement policy (Medigap) to cover the gaps, plus a Part D plan. We compare that path with Medicare Advantage in our guide to choosing between Advantage and Medigap.

When should I sign up?

Your first chance is the Initial Enrollment Period (IEP). It lasts seven months. It starts three months before the month you turn 65, includes your birthday month and ends three months after it.

When your coverage begins depends on when you sign up during that window:

  • Sign up in the three months before your birthday month and coverage starts the first day of your birthday month.
  • Sign up in your birthday month or the three months after and coverage starts the first day of the next month.

One quirk: if your birthday falls on the first of a month, premium-free Part A starts the month before.

If you already collect Social Security or Railroad Retirement benefits, you are usually enrolled in Parts A and B automatically, and your Medicare card comes in the mail. Everyone else signs up through Social Security, online at ssa.gov/medicare or by phone at 1-800-772-1213.

Missed the window?

The General Enrollment Period runs January 1 to March 31 each year. Coverage starts the month after you sign up. You may owe a late penalty unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.

What if I am still working at 65?

Plenty of New Jerseyans keep working, or stay on a working spouse's plan, well past 65. Whether you can safely delay Part B depends mostly on the size of the employer.

Employer with 20 or more employees

The job-based plan usually pays first and Medicare pays second. Many people in this spot take premium-free Part A and delay Part B. When the job or the coverage ends, you get a Special Enrollment Period to sign up for Part B with no penalty. It lasts until eight months after the job or the coverage ends, whichever comes first.

Employer with fewer than 20 employees

Medicare usually pays first. If you skip Part B, the employer plan may refuse to pay claims Medicare would have covered. In most small-employer cases you should enroll in Part B at 65. Ask the plan administrator in writing how it coordinates with Medicare.

Three traps to avoid

  • COBRA and retiree plans do not count. Only coverage based on current work protects you. If you leave a job and pick up COBRA, your eight-month clock is already running.
  • Health savings accounts (HSAs). Once any part of Medicare starts, you cannot put money into an HSA. If you sign up for Part A after 65, it can be backdated up to six months (never before the month you turned 65). Stop HSA contributions about six months before you apply so you do not owe tax on excess contributions.
  • Drug coverage. Ask your employer plan for a letter saying whether its drug coverage is "creditable," meaning at least as good as standard Part D. Keep that letter. You may need it to prove you do not owe a Part D penalty later.

When you sign up for Part B later, Social Security asks for two forms: the CMS-40B application and the CMS-L564, where your employer confirms your coverage. You can also apply online and upload proof, such as W-2s showing pre-tax premiums or pay stubs with premium deductions.

How do the late penalties work?

Medicare's penalties are small at first and add up because they usually last as long as you have the coverage.

  • Part B: 10% added to your premium for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B but did not. Wait two years without a valid reason and you pay 20% extra. In 2026 that turns $202.90 into $243.50 a month.
  • Part D: 1% of the "national base beneficiary premium" for each month you went without Part D or creditable drug coverage. It applies after a gap of 63 days or more. The 2026 base premium is $38.99, so a 14-month gap adds about $5.50 a month on top of your plan premium, for as long as you have Part D.
  • Part A: only matters if you have to buy Part A. The premium can rise 10%, for twice the number of years you delayed.
A penalty that looks like pocket change at 65 can follow you for 25 years.

People who qualify for Extra Help or a Medicare Savings Program generally avoid these penalties. See our guide to prescription and bill help for New Jersey's PAAD and Senior Gold programs.

What will Medicare cost me in 2026?

Item2026 amount
Part B standard monthly premium$202.90
Part B yearly deductible$283
Part A hospital deductible (per benefit period)$1,736
Part A hospital coinsurance, days 61 to 90$434 a day
Skilled nursing facility coinsurance, days 21 to 100$217 a day
Part A premium with 30 to 39 quarters of work$311 a month
Part A premium with fewer than 30 quarters$565 a month
Part D yearly out-of-pocket cap on covered drugs$2,100
Part D standard deductible$615

Higher earners pay more for Part B and Part D through an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA). For 2026 the Part B surcharge starts above $109,000 of modified adjusted gross income for a single filer, or $218,000 for a married couple filing jointly. Social Security uses your tax return from two years earlier. If your income dropped because you retired, you can ask it to use a newer year by filing form SSA-44.

Original Medicare has no yearly cap on what you pay for Part A and Part B services. That is the main reason people buy Medigap or choose a Medicare Advantage plan, which does have a yearly limit. 2027 premiums and deductibles had not been announced when we updated this guide in October 2026. The Medicare Trustees projected a 2027 Part B premium of about $209.50 and a deductible of about $292, but treat those as estimates. Check Medicare.gov before you budget.

A month-by-month timeline

Say you live in Cherry Hill and turn 65 on March 18, 2027. You are retiring from a large employer at the end of February and are not yet collecting Social Security. Your IEP runs December 1, 2026, to June 30, 2027. Here is a sensible plan.

  1. October to November 2026. Create a my Social Security account at ssa.gov. Ask HR for a creditable coverage letter and the date your group coverage ends. List your doctors, hospitals, prescriptions and pharmacy. Book a free SHIP appointment.
  2. December 1, 2026. Your IEP opens. Apply for Parts A and B online. Because you apply before your birthday month, coverage starts March 1, 2027.
  3. January to February 2027. Your Medicare card arrives. Choose your path: Medigap plus a Part D plan, or a Medicare Advantage plan. Enroll so everything starts March 1.
  4. March 1, 2027. Coverage begins. Your six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period also starts now, because you are 65 and have Part B. It runs through August 2027. During it, any Medigap insurer in New Jersey must sell you a policy regardless of your health.
  5. March 2027 to February 2028. Schedule your free Welcome to Medicare preventive visit. You can have it any time in your first 12 months of Part B.
  6. June 30, 2027. Your IEP ends. If you have not signed up by now, the General Enrollment Period and penalties come into play.
  7. October 15 to December 7, 2027. Your first Medicare Open Enrollment as a member. Review your drug plan or Advantage plan for 2028.

If you keep working at a large employer instead, you could take premium-free Part A at 65 (minding the HSA rule) and save Part B for later. Put the end date of your coverage on the calendar and apply at least a month before it.

How can SHIP help me?

New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) offers free, one-on-one Medicare counseling. The Department of Human Services runs it with federal funding, and trained volunteer counselors work in all 21 counties. They do not sell, recommend or endorse any plan, agent or company.

A SHIP counselor can:

  • Explain your enrollment dates and whether you can safely delay Part B.
  • Run your exact prescriptions through the Medicare Plan Finder.
  • Compare Medigap prices using the state's rate charts.
  • Check whether you qualify for help paying premiums.
  • Help sort out a billing problem or a denied claim.

Call the SHIP Information Center at 1-800-792-8820 or your County Office on Aging. Appointments run by phone, by video or in person. Bring your Medicare card (or your application confirmation), your medication list and any letters from your employer plan.

If someone pressures you, offers a gift for your Medicare number or claims to be "from Medicare" on a cold call, hang up. Report it to New Jersey's Senior Medicare Patrol at 1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117. Our scams guide covers the most common tricks.

You may also find our guides to hearing aids and hearing help and affordable dental care helpful.

faq.q: Do I have to sign up for Medicare if I am still working?
faq.a: Not always. If your employer has 20 or more employees and you have coverage through current work, you can usually delay Part B without penalty. Many people still take premium-free Part A. If the employer has fewer than 20 employees, Medicare usually pays first, so you generally need Part B at 65.

faq.q: Is COBRA enough to avoid the Part B penalty?
faq.a: No. COBRA does not count as coverage from current employment. Your eight-month Special Enrollment Period is measured from when the job or the group coverage ends, whichever comes first, even if you then take COBRA.

faq.q: What does Part B cost in 2026?
faq.a: The standard premium is $202.90 a month and the yearly deductible is $283. People with higher incomes pay an extra amount called IRMAA.

faq.q: Can SHIP tell me which plan to buy?
faq.a: SHIP counselors do not sell or endorse plans. They will walk you through your options and run comparisons so you can make your own decision. Call 1-800-792-8820.

faq.q: What happens if I miss my Initial Enrollment Period?
faq.a: You can sign up during the General Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31, with coverage starting the month after you enroll. You may owe a late penalty unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, for example because you had coverage from current work.

faq.q: How much is the Part B late enrollment penalty?
faq.a: It adds 10% to your premium for each full 12 months you could have had Part B but did not, usually for as long as you have Part B. A two-year delay turns the 2026 premium of $202.90 into $243.50 a month.

title: Medicare Advantage or Medigap? How to choose in New Jersey
dek: Open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. Here is how the two paths really differ, the New Jersey Medigap rules most people never hear about, and the questions to ask before you sign.
keyFacts: Medicare Open Enrollment: October 15 to December 7. Changes start January 1.
Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment: January 1 to March 31, one change allowed.
Your best Medigap window is the 6 months after you are 65 and enrolled in Part B. New Jersey has no yearly birthday switch rule.
NJ requires Medigap insurers to offer Plan D to people on Medicare due to disability at ages 50 to 64; Horizon covers those under 50.
The 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap is $2,100 on covered drugs, in either path.
body:
Every fall, Medicare beneficiaries in New Jersey face the same question. Stay with Original Medicare and a Medigap policy, or go with a Medicare Advantage plan? The ads focus on free extras. The bigger questions are how you want to pay for care and how much freedom you want in picking doctors.

Medicare Open Enrollment runs October 15 to December 7, 2026. Any change you make takes effect January 1, 2027. Here is how to think it through.

What is the basic difference?

Path one: Original Medicare plus Medigap plus Part D. Medicare itself pays your doctor and hospital bills. A Medigap policy from a private insurer picks up some or all of what Medicare leaves behind. That can include the Part A deductible and the 20% coinsurance on Part B services. A separate Part D plan covers prescriptions. You can see any doctor or hospital in the country that accepts Medicare. No referrals are needed.

Path two: Medicare Advantage (Part C). A private insurer approved by Medicare covers your Part A and Part B services, and usually your drugs, in one plan. Most plans use networks. Many add dental, vision or hearing benefits and gym memberships. Every Advantage plan has a yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket for covered services.

Original Medicare + Medigap + Part DMedicare Advantage
Monthly premiumsHigher (Part B + Medigap + Part D)Often low or $0 on top of Part B
Costs when you use careLow and predictable, depending on the Medigap planCopays and coinsurance, up to the plan's yearly limit
Choice of doctorsAny provider nationwide that takes MedicareUsually a network; out-of-network care costs more or is not covered
Prior authorizationRareCommon for scans, surgery, rehab and some drugs
Extras (dental, vision, hearing)Not includedOften included, with limits
Switching laterEasy to switch drug plans each fallEasy to switch plans, but moving back to Medigap can be hard

Neither path is right for everyone. A healthy 66-year-old in Toms River with two generic prescriptions may be happy with a low-premium Advantage plan. A 72-year-old in Montclair who sees specialists in Manhattan may value Medigap's freedom more than the premium savings.

What makes Medigap different in New Jersey?

Your six-month window matters most

Federal law gives you a one-time Medigap Open Enrollment Period. It lasts six months and starts the first month you are both 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. During it, any company selling Medigap in New Jersey must sell you any of its policies at its standard rate, whatever your health.

After that window closes, insurers in New Jersey may ask health questions and can turn you down or charge more. Some states give people a yearly chance to switch Medigap plans around their birthday. As of 2026, New Jersey is not one of them. Bills that would let people buy Medigap without health questions at any time (A2301 and S2592) were introduced in the Legislature in 2026, but similar bills have stalled before. Until something passes, the first decision carries a lot of weight here.

In New Jersey, leaving Medigap for Advantage is easy. Coming back can be the hard part.

Guaranteed issue rights later on

You can still buy Medigap without health questions in certain situations. These include your Advantage plan leaving your area, you moving out of its service area, or an employer ending retiree coverage completely. There is also a trial right. If you drop a Medigap policy to try Medicare Advantage for the first time and leave within the first year, you can generally get Medigap back. The same applies if you joined an Advantage plan when you first got Medicare at 65 and leave within 12 months.

Rules for people under 65

Federal law does not guarantee Medigap to people on Medicare because of a disability. New Jersey goes further:

  • Ages 50 to 64: any insurer that sells Medigap to people 65 and over must also offer a policy to people 50 to 64 who are on Medicare because of a disability. For people who became eligible on or after January 1, 2020, that is Plan D (Plan C for those eligible earlier). Apply within your first 12 months of Part B, because after that the company may turn you down. The premium cannot be higher than the company charges people who qualify by age.
  • Under 50: Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield of New Jersey is the state's contracted carrier and must issue Plan D to eligible applicants who apply within 12 months of starting Part B. Horizon's number for this plan is 1-877-234-1240. On the state's May 2026 chart, the under-50 Plan D premium was $181.92 a month for women and $196.16 for men.
  • At 65: you get a fresh six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period and can buy any Medigap plan from any insurer in the state.

New Jersey SHIP publishes current Medigap rate charts for age 65, ages 50 to 64 and under 50. On the August 2026 chart for ages 50 to 64, Horizon's Plan D was $179.92 a month for women and about $194 for men. Rates change, so always confirm with the company.

Will my doctors and hospitals be covered?

This is where New Jersey is different from most states. Many residents get care across the river. North Jersey families often use New York City hospitals. South Jersey families often use Philadelphia health systems.

With Original Medicare, any doctor or hospital in the United States that accepts Medicare will take you. Your Medigap policy follows along. That freedom is a big reason Medigap is popular with people who see out-of-state specialists or spend winters in Florida.

With Medicare Advantage, the network is everything. Watch for these details:

  • HMO plans generally cover only in-network care, except emergencies and urgent care. Many require referrals to see specialists.
  • PPO plans pay something for out-of-network care, at a higher cost to you.
  • Out-of-state systems may be in some New Jersey plans and not others. A plan can include a hospital but leave out the doctors who practice there.
  • Networks change. A doctor in the plan this year may leave next year. Plans can also change benefits each January.

Do not rely on a sales flyer. Call each doctor's billing office and ask: "Are you in network for [exact plan name] for 2027?" Then check the plan's online directory too.

How do I use the Medicare Plan Finder?

The Medicare Plan Finder is the official comparison tool. It shows every Part D and Medicare Advantage plan in your ZIP code with estimated yearly costs.

  1. Log in or continue as a guest. Logging in at Medicare.gov pulls in your drug list automatically. Guest mode works fine too.
  2. Enter your ZIP code and county. Plans in Cape May differ from plans in Bergen.
  3. Add every prescription with the exact dose. This is the step that changes the answer most.
  4. Pick one or two pharmacies. Prices often differ between preferred and standard pharmacies, and mail order.
  5. Sort by total drug and premium cost. Look past the premium. A $0 plan can cost more by year's end.
  6. Open the plan details. Check the deductible, copays for specialists and hospital stays, the out-of-pocket limit and the star rating.
  7. Write down your top two or three choices. Then verify doctors by phone before you enroll.

Stuck? A SHIP counselor will run Plan Finder with you for free at 1-800-792-8820. You can also call Medicare at 1-800-633-4227.

What if I change my mind?

You have more than one chance each year.

  • Medicare Open Enrollment, October 15 to December 7. Anyone can switch Advantage plans, move between Advantage and Original Medicare, or change Part D plans. Changes start January 1.
  • Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment, January 1 to March 31. Only for people already in an Advantage plan. You get one change: move to a different Advantage plan, or leave Advantage for Original Medicare and add a Part D plan. The change starts the first of the next month.

Here is the catch. Leaving Advantage during either window does not by itself give you a right to buy Medigap in New Jersey. Unless your trial right or another guaranteed issue situation applies, the insurer can ask health questions. Before you drop an Advantage plan, apply for the Medigap policy and wait for approval.

What questions should I ask before I enroll?

  • Are all my doctors and my preferred hospitals in network for next year, by name?
  • What is the yearly out-of-pocket limit, and what would a hospital stay cost me?
  • Which services need prior authorization? How do I appeal a denial?
  • Are all my drugs on the formulary? What tier, and are there quantity limits or step therapy rules?
  • What do the dental, vision and hearing benefits really cover, and what is the dollar cap?
  • Does the plan cover care when I travel or spend winters out of state?
  • For Medigap: which plan letter, and how has this company raised rates in recent years?
  • Am I in a guaranteed issue window right now, or will I face health questions?
Watch the 2026 drug cap

In 2026, Part D caps what you pay for covered drugs at $2,100 for the year. This applies to stand-alone plans and Advantage drug coverage alike. The maximum Part D deductible is $615. Check how 2027 plans handle your drugs before December 7.

New to Medicare this year? Start with our Medicare 101 guide. If premiums are a strain, PAAD and Senior Gold may help.

faq.q: When can I switch from Medicare Advantage back to Original Medicare?
faq.a: During Medicare Open Enrollment (October 15 to December 7) or the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period (January 1 to March 31). Getting a Medigap policy is a separate step, and outside a guaranteed issue situation the insurer in New Jersey may ask health questions.

faq.q: Does New Jersey have a Medigap birthday rule?
faq.a: No. As of 2026 New Jersey does not give a yearly birthday window to switch Medigap plans without health questions. Your six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period at 65 is the key window.

faq.q: I am on Medicare due to disability and I am 58. Can I buy Medigap?
faq.a: Yes. In New Jersey, insurers that sell Medigap must offer Plan D to people who became eligible at 50 to 64, if you apply within 12 months of starting Part B. The premium cannot exceed what the company charges a 65-year-old.

faq.q: Can I use New York or Philadelphia hospitals?
faq.a: With Original Medicare, yes, at any hospital that accepts Medicare. With a Medicare Advantage plan, it depends on the plan's network. Confirm each hospital and doctor by name with the plan before you enroll.

faq.q: When is Medicare open enrollment for 2027 coverage?
faq.a: October 15 to December 7, 2026. Any change you make takes effect January 1, 2027. People already in a Medicare Advantage plan get one more change from January 1 to March 31.

title: NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS: how Medicaid pays for long-term care
dek: Medicare does not pay for long-term care. In New Jersey, Medicaid's MLTSS program can, at home, in assisted living or in a nursing home. Here are the 2026 limits, the five-year look-back and how to apply.
keyFacts: 2026 MLTSS income limit: $2,982 a month for the applicant. Higher incomes may qualify with a Qualified Income Trust.
Asset limit for a single applicant: $2,000. A spouse at home can keep up to $162,660.
Transfers in the 60 months before you apply are reviewed. The NJ penalty divisor is $420.67 a day.
You must need nursing-home-level care, now or within 30 days.
Start with your county ADRC: 1-877-222-3737.
body:
Many families find out the hard way that Medicare does not pay for ongoing help with bathing, dressing or meals. It covers short rehab stays and some home health visits after an illness. It does not cover long-term custodial care. In New Jersey, the program that does is Medicaid, known here as NJ FamilyCare, through a benefit called Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS).

The rules are detailed and the paperwork is heavy. Families who understand the basics early tend to avoid the costly mistakes. Here is what you need to know.

What is MLTSS and who is it for?

MLTSS delivers long-term care through private health plans, called managed care organizations (MCOs), that contract with NJ FamilyCare. Each member gets a care manager who helps plan services. You may qualify if you:

  • Are 65 or older, or under 65 and determined blind or disabled by Social Security or the State of New Jersey.
  • Live in New Jersey and are a U.S. citizen or qualified noncitizen.
  • Need nursing-home-level care now or within 30 days (the clinical test).
  • Meet NJ FamilyCare's income and asset rules, including the five-year look-back (the financial test).

Five MCOs offer MLTSS: Aetna Better Health of New Jersey, Amerigroup New Jersey, Horizon NJ Health, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan and WellCare Health Plans of New Jersey. All five serve every county except that WellCare does not serve Hunterdon. To ask about choosing or changing a plan, call 1-866-472-5338 (TTY 1-800-701-0720).

What are the financial limits in 2026?

These are the key numbers for long-term care Medicaid in New Jersey. Federal standards change every January, and some spousal figures change in July.

Rule2026 figure
Applicant's monthly income limit (300% of the SSI benefit of $994)$2,982
Countable assets, single applicant$2,000
Assets a spouse at home may keep (Community Spouse Resource Allowance)Half the couple's assets, at least $32,532 and at most $162,660
Minimum monthly income for a spouse at home (from July 1, 2026)$2,705
Maximum monthly income allowance for a spouse at home$4,066.50
Home equity limit (if you live there or plan to return)$1,130,000
Look-back period for transfers60 months
Penalty divisor (April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027)$420.67 a day

What if income is over $2,982?

You may still qualify. New Jersey lets applicants put the income above the limit into a Qualified Income Trust, sometimes called a Miller Trust. The money in the trust then goes toward the cost of care. Setting one up correctly matters, so most families use an elder law attorney.

What counts as an asset?

Bank accounts, CDs, stocks, bonds, most retirement accounts and cash value life insurance usually count. Your home generally does not count while you or your spouse lives there, as long as your equity is under the limit. One car and a prepaid, irrevocable funeral arrangement are commonly excluded too. Ask the county agency before you spend down, because the details matter.

Not ready for long-term care?

Regular NJ FamilyCare for aged, blind and disabled adults covers doctor visits, hospital care and prescriptions. Its 2026 income limit is about $1,330 a month for one person (100% of the federal poverty level), with assets up to $4,000 for one person and $6,000 for a couple.

How does the five-year look-back period work?

When you apply for MLTSS, the state reviews every transfer you made in the 60 months before your application. It is looking for money or property you gave away, or sold for less than it was worth.

If it finds one, you face a penalty period when Medicaid will not pay for your long-term care. The state divides the amount transferred by the penalty divisor. Say a widow in Toms River gave her grandson $42,067 toward a house three years before applying. $42,067 divided by $420.67 equals 100 days without Medicaid coverage for her care. The penalty clock starts only after she is otherwise eligible, which is often when savings are gone.

Birthday checks, tuition help and "loans" to children can all show up in a look-back review.

Some transfers are allowed, such as transfers between spouses. Others depend on the facts, like transfers to a disabled child or a caregiver child who lived in the home. If you are thinking about giving money away, talk to an elder law attorney first. Our estate planning guide explains how to find one.

Keep in mind that New Jersey may seek repayment from the estate of a member who was 55 or older for services Medicaid paid for. This is called estate recovery. Ask about it when you plan.

How spousal protections work: an example

Example: a couple in Edison

Say your husband, 84, needs nursing home care and you, 80, stay in your home. You have $300,000 in countable savings between you, plus the house. Half is $150,000, which is under the $162,660 cap, so you keep $150,000 and the house. Most of the other $150,000 must be spent on his care or other allowed costs before he qualifies. He can keep $2,000. If your own income is below $2,705 a month, part of his income can be shifted to you to bring you up toward that amount. These numbers are hypothetical. An elder law attorney can check the details for your case.

What does clinical eligibility mean?

Being old enough and poor enough is not enough. You also have to need nursing-home-level care. In practice, that usually means needing hands-on help with several activities of daily living, such as bathing, dressing, toileting, moving from bed to chair or eating. Significant cognitive impairment, as with dementia, can also qualify.

A trained assessor visits in person and uses the state's assessment tool. The state's Office of Community Choice Options makes the clinical decision. Before the visit, write down every task your parent needs help with and how often. Families often understate needs out of pride. Be honest and specific.

What does MLTSS cover at home, in assisted living and in a nursing home?

The care plan is built around assessed need. Services can include:

  • At home: personal care assistants, home health aides, adult day health, respite for family caregivers, home-delivered meals, a personal emergency response system, home modifications such as grab bars or ramps, and vehicle modifications.
  • Assisted living and community residential services: care services in a participating residence. Members generally contribute most of their income toward the cost, and not every assisted living residence accepts Medicaid. Some require a period of private pay first, so ask before you move in.
  • Nursing home care: full coverage in a Medicaid-certified facility. Most of the resident's income goes toward the bill, minus a small personal needs allowance.
  • Behavioral health: mental health and addiction services.

Most people prefer to stay home. MLTSS was built partly to make that possible. Read our aging in place guide for other ways to stay home safely.

What is PACE, and is it in my county?

The Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) is another option. A PACE organization runs a day center with doctors, nurses, therapists, social workers and transportation, and it handles all of your care. Medicare and Medicaid pay for it. To join, you must be 55 or older, need nursing-home-level care, be able to live safely in the community with PACE services and live in the program's service area.

In January 2026 the state announced funding to bring PACE to all 21 counties. Programs open in stages, so check availability for your ZIP code. Programs the state lists as operating:

  • AtlantiCare LIFE Connection (Atlantic City): Atlantic and Cape May counties
  • BoldAge PACE (Lakehurst): Ocean County
  • BoldAge PACE (Oceanport): Monmouth County
  • Capital Health LIFE (Bordentown): Mercer County and parts of Burlington
  • Inspira LIFE (Vineland and Williamstown): Cumberland, Gloucester and Salem counties
  • BoldAge PACE (East Brunswick): Middlesex County
  • Lutheran Senior LIFE at Jersey City: most of Hudson County
  • Lutheran Senior LIFE at Union (Plainfield): Union County
  • Trinity Health LIFE New Jersey (Pennsauken): most of Camden County and parts of Burlington

Programs are still being built for Essex, Bergen, Somerset and Passaic counties. WelbeHealth was chosen for Sussex, Warren and Morris counties, and Senior LIFE for Hunterdon County. The state keeps a current list on its PACE page.

What mistakes cost families the most?

  • Waiting for a crisis. Applications take time. Families who gather records before a hospital discharge have far more choices.
  • Giving money away to qualify. Gifts in the last five years can trigger a penalty period. Get advice first.
  • Missing records. Unexplained withdrawals from bank statements slow down or derail approval. Keep receipts for large purchases.
  • Spending down the wrong way. Paying off debts, repairing the home you live in or buying an irrevocable prepaid funeral can often be allowed. Cash handed to relatives usually is not.
  • Assuming assisted living will take Medicaid. Ask each residence, in writing, whether it accepts MLTSS and whether it requires private pay first.
  • Ignoring the spouse at home. The spousal rules exist to protect the person who stays home. Make sure the application asks for every allowance.

How do I apply?

Applying is a two-track process. One track checks finances. The other checks care needs.

  1. Call your county ADRC. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection is the front door. Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county. Staff will screen your needs and explain options, including PACE.
  2. Apply for NJ FamilyCare. Apply online, by mail or through your County Welfare Agency (Board of Social Services). For help with the aged, blind and disabled application, call 1-800-356-1561.
  3. Gather records. Expect to provide ID, proof of citizenship and New Jersey residence, Medicare and insurance cards, proof of all income, and statements for every bank and investment account. Have up to five years of statements ready for the look-back.
  4. Complete the clinical assessment. A nurse or trained assessor will schedule a visit.
  5. Choose an MCO. Once approved, you pick one of the five health plans. A care manager will build a plan of care with you.
  6. Respond fast. Answer every letter from the county by its deadline. Missed requests for information are a common reason for delays and denials.

If you are denied, the notice explains your right to a fair hearing and the deadline to ask for one. Ask for help from an elder law attorney or Legal Services of New Jersey. For caregivers juggling all this, our respite guide may help you catch your breath.

You may also find our guide to getting paid as a family caregiver helpful.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a nursing home?
faq.a: Only for short skilled stays after a qualifying hospital stay, up to 100 days with a daily coinsurance after day 20. It does not pay for long-term custodial care. In New Jersey, Medicaid through MLTSS is the main public payer for long-term care.

faq.q: What is the 2026 income limit for MLTSS?
faq.a: $2,982 a month for the applicant. If income is higher, a Qualified Income Trust may allow you to qualify.

faq.q: Will my spouse be left with nothing?
faq.a: No. A spouse who stays at home can keep half of the couple's countable assets, between $32,532 and $162,660 in 2026, plus the home in most cases, and may receive part of the applicant's income to reach a minimum monthly amount.

faq.q: Can I get MLTSS at home instead of a nursing home?
faq.a: Yes. MLTSS covers personal care, home health aides, adult day health, home-delivered meals, respite and home modifications based on your assessed needs.

faq.q: Where do I start?
faq.a: Call your county Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. They can screen you, explain MLTSS and PACE, and point you to your County Welfare Agency to apply.

faq.q: How far back does the Medicaid look-back go in New Jersey?
faq.a: Five years, or 60 months, before the date you apply. Gifts or sales below fair value in that window can lead to a penalty period, figured by dividing the amount by $420.67 a day for applications from April 2026 through March 2027.

title: Staying well in New Jersey: falls, checkups, hearing and more
dek: Free balance classes, the Medicare checkups you are already paying for, cheaper hearing aids, and where to turn in a heat wave or a hard month. A practical wellness guide for New Jerseyans 60 and up.
keyFacts: About 1 in 4 adults 65 and older report a fall each year, per the CDC.
A Matter of Balance runs as 8 two-hour sessions for adults 60+ in selected NJ counties. Help finding a class: 609-438-4797.
Medicare's yearly Wellness visit costs $0 when your provider accepts assignment.
OTC hearing aids have been sold without a prescription since October 17, 2022. NJ's HAAAD program reimburses up to $500 per aid for eligible residents.
In crisis, call or text 988. NJ MentalHealthCares: 1-866-202-4357, live help 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
body:
Staying well after 60 comes down to a handful of habits. Keep your balance. Use the checkups you already pay for. Fix your hearing before it isolates you. Plan for the hottest and coldest days. Know who to call when your mood dips.

New Jersey has free or low-cost help for each of these. Most of it runs through your county Office on Aging, which you can reach through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

Why should falls be my first priority?

Falls are the leading cause of injury for adults 65 and older, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). About 1 in 4 older adults report falling each year. That is more than 14 million people nationwide. The CDC also reports that the fall death rate among older adults rose 21% between 2018 and 2024.

Many falls are preventable. The biggest risk factors are weak legs, poor balance, some medications, poor vision and hazards at home. Fear of falling is a risk factor too. People who are afraid move less, get weaker and then fall more.

Three steps make a real difference:

  • Ask your doctor or pharmacist to review your medicines. Sleep aids, some blood pressure drugs and medicines that cause dizziness raise your risk.
  • Get your eyes checked and update your glasses.
  • Make your home safer. Add grab bars, railings on both sides of stairs, night lights and nonslip mats. Remove throw rugs. Our aging in place guide has a room-by-room checklist.

Where can I take a free or low-cost balance class?

New Jersey's Division of Aging Services supports several health promotion programs through county agencies, senior centers, libraries and senior housing.

A Matter of Balance

This program, developed at Boston University, helps people who worry about falling. It meets for eight two-hour sessions in groups of 10 to 12. You learn to see falls as preventable, set realistic goals, make your home safer and do gentle exercises for strength and balance. It is designed for adults 60 and older who can walk on their own. It runs only in selected counties. Call 609-438-4797 for help finding a class, or check the state's contact list on the A Matter of Balance page.

Tai Chi for Arthritis

Tai chi uses slow, flowing movements that build leg strength and balance. Tai Chi for Arthritis, from the Tai Chi for Health Institute, is offered by some county aging offices and senior centers. For example, the Warren County Division of Aging and Disability Services lists tai chi classes at 908-475-6591. Availability changes by season, so ask your county Office on Aging or search NJ 211.

Other state-supported programs

  • Move Today: a 30 to 45 minute non-aerobic class for flexibility, balance and stamina.
  • Otago Exercise Program: a fall prevention exercise and walking program led by a physical therapist.
  • Project Healthy Bones: exercise and education for people with or at risk of osteoporosis.
  • Take Control of Your Health: peer-led workshops for people living with chronic conditions, and their caregivers.
The best balance class is the one close enough that you will keep going.

Which checkups does Medicare cover for free?

Many people on Medicare never use the preventive visits they are entitled to.

  • Welcome to Medicare preventive visit. Once, within your first 12 months of Part B. It reviews your history, checks your body mass index (BMI), includes a simple vision test, screens for depression risk and gives you a written plan of screenings and shots.
  • Yearly Wellness visit. Once every 12 months after that. It includes a health risk questionnaire, a review of your medicines, a cognitive check for signs of dementia and a written prevention plan. You pay nothing if your provider accepts assignment.
Wellness visit or physical?

The yearly Wellness visit is a planning conversation. It does not include a head-to-toe physical exam. If your doctor adds tests or treats a problem during the same visit, you may owe a copay or coinsurance. Original Medicare does not cover a routine physical. Ask the office how the visit will be billed.

How to get the most from your Wellness visit

  • Bring every pill bottle, including vitamins and over-the-counter remedies, or an up-to-date list.
  • Write down any falls or near-falls in the past year, even ones that did not cause an injury.
  • Mention changes in memory, sleep, mood, hearing or vision. Small changes are easier to address early.
  • Ask which screenings and vaccines you are due for, and get the written checklist.
  • Bring a copy of your advance directive, or ask how to start one.

Vaccines

Part B covers flu, pneumococcal and COVID-19 shots, plus hepatitis B for people at medium or high risk. Part D covers recommended adult vaccines such as shingles (Shingrix), RSV for eligible adults and Tdap, with no cost sharing. Many New Jersey pharmacies give these shots. Bring your Medicare card and your Part D or Advantage card.

What about hearing and vision?

Hearing

Untreated hearing loss makes conversation tiring and can pull people away from friends and family. Since October 17, 2022, adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss can buy over-the-counter (OTC) hearing aids in stores or online. No exam or prescription is required. If your loss seems severe, or one ear is much worse than the other, see an audiologist or ear, nose and throat doctor first.

Before you buy an OTC device, check the return window and the warranty. Look for a model you can adjust through an app or buttons. Give yourself a few weeks to get used to it, since the brain takes time to adapt to sounds it has been missing. If it still does not help, return it and get a professional hearing test.

Original Medicare does not pay for hearing aids. Some Medicare Advantage plans include a hearing aid benefit. New Jersey's Hearing Aid Assistance for the Aged and Disabled (HAAAD) program reimburses up to $500 for one hearing aid or $1,000 for two in a calendar year. You must be enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline. The 2026 income limits are $54,943 for a single person and $62,390 for a married couple. Questions go to 1-800-792-9745. See our PAAD guide to apply.

Vision

Medicare does not cover routine eye exams for glasses or contact lenses. It does cover certain medical eye care, such as eye exams for people with diabetes, glaucoma tests for people at high risk and cataract surgery. Many Advantage plans include a yearly eye exam and an eyewear allowance. Check your plan's details during open enrollment.

Vaccines at a glance

VaccineCovered byTypical cost
Flu, COVID-19, pneumococcalPart B$0 if the provider accepts assignment
Hepatitis B (medium or high risk)Part B$0 if the provider accepts assignment
Shingles (Shingrix), RSV, TdapPart D or your Advantage drug coverageUsually $0 at an in-network pharmacy

If you have no Part D plan or drug coverage, you may pay full price for Part D vaccines. Ask the pharmacy to check your coverage before the shot.

How do I stay safe in heat and cold?

Older bodies handle heat less well, and a long New Jersey heat wave can be dangerous. Some medicines, including certain heart, blood pressure and mental health drugs, make it harder to stay cool.

  • Stay in air conditioning during the hottest part of the day. If you do not have it, go to a library, mall or senior center.
  • Find a cooling center through your town or at nj211.org. You can also dial 2-1-1.
  • Drink water before you feel thirsty. Keep taking your medicines, and ask your doctor whether any raise your heat risk.
  • Call 911 for confusion, a very high body temperature, fainting or hot, dry skin. These can signal heat stroke.

In winter, New Jersey law requires a Code Blue alert when the forecast calls for temperatures of 32 degrees or lower, or a wind chill of zero or below for two hours or more. Participating towns open warming centers. If your heat is off or you cannot afford fuel, the state's energy assistance application opened October 1, 2026. See our food and utility help guide.

Have your furnace checked each fall and keep working carbon monoxide and smoke alarms on every level of your home.

Where can I turn for mental health support?

Depression is not a normal part of aging, and it is treatable. Loss, illness, caregiving and loneliness can all weigh on mood. Medicare covers depression screening and outpatient mental health care, including therapy with many licensed counselors.

  • 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Call or text 988, any time, for yourself or someone you are worried about.
  • NJ MentalHealthCares. Run by the Mental Health Association in New Jersey, this free and confidential helpline offers information and referrals. Call 1-866-202-4357. Live help is available 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and you can leave a message after hours.
  • NJ 211. Dial 2-1-1 or 1-877-652-1148 for local counseling, support groups and services.

Who do I call?

Keep this list by the phone or on the fridge.

Medicare questions and plan comparisonsSHIP1-800-792-8820
Hearing aid help, PAAD, LifelineNJSave and PAAD hotline1-800-792-9745
Cooling and warming centers, local helpNJ 211Dial 2-1-1
Mental health information and referralsNJ MentalHealthCares1-866-202-4357
Crisis support, any time988 Suicide and Crisis LifelineCall or text 988

Staying connected protects mental health too. A weekly class, a volunteer shift or a standing coffee date can do a lot. Our staying connected guide and learning guide have ideas near you.

You may also find our guides to hearing aids and hearing help and affordable dental care helpful.

faq.q: Are fall prevention classes free in New Jersey?
faq.a: Many are free or low cost through county Offices on Aging, senior centers and libraries. Cost varies by location. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 or, for A Matter of Balance, 609-438-4797.

faq.q: Is the Medicare yearly Wellness visit really free?
faq.a: Yes, if your provider accepts assignment. You may owe a copay if the doctor also treats a problem or orders tests that are not part of the preventive benefit.

faq.q: Can I buy hearing aids without seeing a doctor?
faq.a: Yes. Since October 17, 2022, adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss can buy OTC hearing aids without a prescription. See a professional if your loss seems severe or sudden.

faq.q: Who can I call if I am feeling depressed or overwhelmed?
faq.a: In a crisis, call or text 988. For information and referrals, call NJ MentalHealthCares at 1-866-202-4357, live help 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover the shingles vaccine?
faq.a: Yes, through Part D or the drug coverage in a Medicare Advantage plan. It is usually $0 at an in-network pharmacy. Flu, COVID-19 and pneumococcal shots are covered by Part B.

faq.q: Does New Jersey help pay for hearing aids?
faq.a: Yes. The HAAAD program reimburses up to $500 for one hearing aid or $1,000 for two in a calendar year if you are enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline. Call 1-800-792-9745.

title: Hearing aids for older adults in New Jersey
dek: Over the counter hearing aids, what Medicare covers, and New Jersey programs that help pay for hearing aids and phones.
keyFacts: OTC hearing aids are for adults 18+ with perceived mild to moderate loss.
Original Medicare doesn't cover hearing aids or fitting exams.
HAAAD repays up to $500 for one hearing aid or $1,000 for two.
DDHH gives free phones and alert devices to eligible residents.
body:
Hearing usually fades so slowly that the people around you notice before you do. The TV creeps louder, restaurants get harder, and phone calls become a chore. The good news is that help costs less than it used to. Since 2022 you can buy hearing aids off the shelf, and New Jersey has its own programs that pay part or all of the bill for people on modest incomes. This guide walks through your options, from a first hearing test to free equipment for your phone.

What are the signs of hearing loss?

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says about one third of older adults have hearing loss. The National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) puts it at about one in three people ages 65 to 74, and nearly half of people over 75. Common signs include:

  • You often ask people to repeat themselves.
  • You have trouble following a conversation when two or more people are talking.
  • Phone calls are hard to understand, or background noise drowns out speech.
  • It seems like other people mumble, or children's and higher voices are hard to catch.
  • Family members complain that the TV is too loud.

Ringing, buzzing or hissing in the ears (tinnitus) is also common and can be an early sign of hearing loss.

Why does treating hearing loss matter?

The NIA says older adults with hearing loss have a higher risk of dementia, and their memory and concentration tend to decline faster. People who use hearing aids or cochlear implants show less long term decline. Hearing loss can also lead to withdrawal, loneliness and depression, and even mild loss is linked to a higher risk of falls. The NIDCD adds that it can make it hard to follow a doctor's advice or hear warnings. Left alone, hearing problems can get worse. If isolation is part of the picture, our guide to staying connected in New Jersey has more ideas, and healthy aging in New Jersey covers the bigger picture.

Are over the counter hearing aids right for me?

Since October 17, 2022, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has allowed hearing aids to be sold over the counter (OTC), in stores and online, with no exam or prescription. They are meant for adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss. "Perceived" means you judge it yourself. The FDA lists these signs that an OTC aid may fit:

  • Speech is hard to hear in noisy places or in groups.
  • You have trouble hearing on the phone.
  • Listening leaves you tired.
  • Others say the TV or radio is too loud.

OTC aids are not meant for severe loss. If you can't hear speech even in a quiet room, or you have trouble hearing loud sounds like power tools or loud music, see a hearing professional instead.

See a doctor first if any of these apply

The FDA and NIDCD say to see a doctor, preferably an ear, nose and throat specialist, if your hearing changed suddenly or got worse quickly, if one ear is much worse than the other, if you hear ringing in only one ear, if you have dizziness or spinning with hearing loss, if you have ear pain, or if you've had fluid, pus or blood from the ear in the past six months. Heavy earwax or something stuck in the ear also needs a doctor.

What does Medicare pay for?

Original Medicare does not cover hearing aids, and it does not cover exams for fitting hearing aids. That surprises many people.

Medicare Part B does cover diagnostic hearing and balance exams when your doctor or another provider orders them to see whether you need treatment. You can also see an audiologist once every 12 months without an order, for gradual hearing loss and some other conditions. After the Part B deductible you pay 20% of the Medicare approved amount, plus a copayment if the exam is in a hospital outpatient department.

Medicare Advantage plans may offer extra benefits that Original Medicare doesn't cover, including some hearing services. Benefits differ from plan to plan, so read the plan's details before you choose. Our guides to turning 65 and Medicare and Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap explain the trade offs.

How does New Jersey's HAAAD program help?

Hearing Aid Assistance to the Aged and Disabled (HAAAD) is a state program that pays you back for part of what you spend on hearing aids. It reimburses up to $500 for one hearing aid or up to $1,000 for two in a calendar year. Batteries and repairs are not covered. If you buy a hearing aid in a later year, you file a new application.

To qualify you must:

  • Have hearing loss and live in New Jersey.
  • Be 65 or older, or 18 to 64 and receiving Social Security Disability benefits.
  • Have 2026 income no higher than $54,943 if single or $62,390 if married.
  • Be enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline. If you aren't, you must file an NJSave application first.

You can't get HAAAD money if Medicaid, another insurer or retirement benefits already pay for your hearing aids. If that coverage is only partial, you may still get some help.

  1. Get into PAAD first. If you aren't enrolled, apply through NJSave. That one form also checks you for Senior Gold, Lifeline and other help. Call 1-800-792-9745.
  2. Buy after approval. Your hearing aid receipt must be dated on or after the date of your PAAD approval.
  3. Gather your papers. You need the receipt and either a written statement from your doctor that the hearing aid is medically necessary or a copy of the hearing aid prescription.
  4. Apply. Print the application from the HAAAD page and mail the signed copy to HAAAD, PO Box 715, Trenton, NJ 08625-0715, or fax it to 609-588-2528. Checks usually arrive six to eight weeks after you're found eligible.

Thinking about an OTC hearing aid? Call before you buy to ask whether it will qualify, since HAAAD asks for a doctor's statement or prescription.

Can I get free hearing aids in New Jersey?

Possibly. The state's Division of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DDHH) runs the New Jersey Hearing Aid Project with Montclair State University. It gives free refurbished hearing aids to New Jersey residents who are 65 or older (or receive Social Security Disability) and whose 2026 income is no more than $54,943 single or $62,390 married. PAAD members use application Form A. Everyone else uses Form B.

If you have NJ FamilyCare (New Jersey's Medicaid), DDHH says hearing aids are covered by Medicaid and NJ FamilyCare plans except Plan D, including two hearing aids. Ask your health plan how to get them, or call NJ FamilyCare at 1-800-701-0710.

Veterans should start with the VA. DDHH's resource list says any Veteran enrolled and eligible for VA health care is eligible for hearing aids. In New Jersey, the VA medical centers are in East Orange (973-676-1000) and Lyons (908-647-0180). Veterans who get their hearing aids from the VA and are registered at a VA medical center can also order free batteries and accessories.

What if the phone is the hardest part?

DDHH's Equipment Distribution Program gives free devices to New Jersey residents with hearing loss whose household income is no more than 400% of the federal poverty level. On the October 2026 application that is $63,840 for one person and $86,560 for two. A treating provider must certify that you'll benefit. Choices include amplified phones, personal amplifiers, TV listening systems, flashing or vibrating alerts, and a smartphone or tablet loaded with captioning apps. You pay any cell plan. Devices depend on supply and funding.

Captioned phone service is another option. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) explains that Internet Protocol Captioned Telephone Service (IP CTS) shows the other person's words as text on a screen while you talk. It is for people with hearing loss who can speak and have some hearing left. It works with a captioned phone or your existing phone plus a computer or other web device. The FCC says relay services like this cost users nothing.

Who can I call?

NJ FamilyCare1-800-701-0710
VA New Jersey Health Care SystemEast Orange 973-676-1000, Lyons 908-647-0180

For anyone, a good first step is telling your doctor what you've noticed.

faq.q: Do I need a hearing test to buy an over the counter hearing aid?
faq.a: No. OTC hearing aids are sold without an exam or prescription to adults 18 and older with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss. See a doctor first if your hearing changed suddenly, one ear is worse, or you have pain, dizziness or drainage.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for hearing aids?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not cover hearing aids or exams to fit them. Part B covers diagnostic hearing and balance exams in some cases. Some Medicare Advantage plans include hearing benefits, so check the plan details.

faq.q: How much does HAAAD pay in New Jersey?
faq.a: Up to $500 for one hearing aid or $1,000 for two in a calendar year. You must be enrolled in PAAD or Lifeline. If you aren't, file an NJSave application first. Call 1-800-792-9745.

faq.q: What is the 2026 income limit for HAAAD?
faq.a: $54,943 for a single person and $62,390 for a married couple, the same as PAAD.

title: Affordable dental care for older adults in NJ
dek: Medicare pays for very little dental work. Here is what it does cover, what NJ FamilyCare includes, and where New Jersey seniors can find low-cost or free dental care.
keyFacts: Original Medicare doesn't cover routine cleanings, fillings, extractions or dentures.
NJ FamilyCare covers adult exams, cleanings, fillings, extractions and dentures.
Rutgers School of Dental Medicine in Newark: (973) 972-4242.
Donated Dental Services offers free care to New Jerseyans over 65 who can't afford it.
body:
A sore tooth or a loose denture can make it hard to eat well, speak clearly and feel like yourself. Dental care also gets expensive fast, and many people are surprised to learn how little Medicare pays for it. The good news is that New Jersey has real options, from NJ FamilyCare to a dental school in Newark to volunteer dentists who treat older adults for free. This guide walks through each one.

Does Medicare cover dental care?

Mostly no. Medicare.gov says Original Medicare doesn't cover routine dental services like cleanings, fillings and tooth extractions, and it doesn't cover dentures. You pay the full cost of those services.

There are a few narrow exceptions. Medicare may pay for dental care that is tied to a covered medical treatment, such as:

  • An oral exam and dental treatment before a heart valve replacement, an organ transplant or a bone marrow transplant.
  • Treating a mouth infection before cancer treatment like chemotherapy, and treating complications during head and neck cancer treatment.
  • Dental or oral exams, and treatment to remove an oral or dental infection, before and during dialysis for End-Stage Renal Disease.
  • Some dental services you get during a hospital stay, because of your medical condition or how serious the procedure is.

When Part B covers one of these services, you generally pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible, plus a facility copayment if you're treated in a hospital outpatient setting.

Can a Medicare Advantage plan help?

It can. The federal Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) notes that Medicare Advantage plans often include dental benefits. What they cover varies a great deal from plan to plan, so read the dental section of any plan's benefits summary before you enroll, and check that your dentist is in the network. Our guide to Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap explains the tradeoffs, and turning 65 and Medicare covers the basics if you're new to it.

What dental care does NJ FamilyCare cover for adults?

NJ FamilyCare, New Jersey's Medicaid program, lists dental care among its covered services. A state flyer for adult NJ FamilyCare members (an older document, so confirm details with your plan) lists:

  • Oral exams twice a year (more often if medically necessary), plus emergency exams.
  • X-rays to check for cavities and other problems.
  • Cleanings and fluoride treatments twice a year.
  • Fillings in tooth-colored or silver material.
  • Crowns, gum treatment, root canals and complete or partial dentures. These may need approval first.
  • Tooth extractions and other oral surgery.

Cosmetic work isn't covered. To find a dentist, call the dental number on your NJ FamilyCare ID card or use your health plan's online dentist list. If you're not in a health plan, the flyer says to call for help finding a dentist. NJ FamilyCare's number is 1-800-701-0710 (TTY 711). If you're not sure whether you qualify, see our guide to NJ FamilyCare for seniors.

Can I get care at the Rutgers dental school?

Yes. HRSA points out that dental schools often run clinics with lower-cost care, where students treat patients under the supervision of licensed professionals. In New Jersey, that's the Rutgers School of Dental Medicine in Newark. The state's NJ Basic Needs page describes it as a full range of oral health services at an affordable cost, and says it accepts Medicaid but not private insurance.

  • Getting started: call (973) 972-4242 for an initial evaluation appointment, or use the online request form on the school's site. Rutgers says there is a fee for this first visit, which includes an exam, X-rays and a talk about the treatment you need. Ask what it costs when you call.
  • Questions about being assigned to a student: Patient Screening, (973) 972-7370.
  • Dental emergencies: people who aren't current patients can walk in to the Newark student and graduate specialty clinics on a first come, first served basis. Arrive by 9 a.m. for the morning session or by 1 p.m. for the afternoon.

The school's clinics are at 110 Bergen Street in Newark. Rutgers also runs a faculty practice in the Doctor's Office Center at 90 Bergen Street, Suite 7700, open Monday to Thursday 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Friday 8 a.m. to noon, with free validated parking in the garage at Bergen Street and 12th Avenue. School clinics can take more visits than a private office, so plan for that.

Where else can I find low-cost dental care?

Community health centers. HRSA funds health centers that may offer dental care, and at many of them the cost is based on your income. Look for one near you with HRSA's free Find a Health Center tool. When you call, HRSA suggests asking, "Do you offer discounts based on income?" That's called a sliding fee discount.

Donated Dental Services. Dental Lifeline Network runs this volunteer program in New Jersey, where dentists treat people for free. You must have no means to afford dental care and be over 65, permanently disabled, or need medically necessary dental care. It doesn't cover emergency or cosmetic work. Apply online or by mail through dentallifeline.org/new-jersey. The program's coordinators are at 973-967-9171 for northern New Jersey and 732-821-3056 for the rest of the state. When we checked in October 2026, the program said it was not accepting applications from Ocean County, with exceptions for qualifying veterans and for people whose doctor documents that a dental problem is blocking needed medical treatment.

Veterans. VA dental care isn't automatic for every veteran. According to the VA, veterans who can get any needed dental care include those with a service-connected dental disability rated 10% or more, former prisoners of war, and those with service-connected disabilities rated 100% (or paid at the 100% rate because they can't work). Other groups qualify for limited care, such as treatment for a dental problem that is making a service-connected condition worse. Call the VA at 1-877-222-8387 or ask your nearest VA facility to check your eligibility. The VA also points veterans to its VA Dental Insurance Program (VADIP) for dental insurance.

For more ways to save on health costs, see free and discounted help in New Jersey.

Why does oral health matter more as we age?

Losing teeth is common, but it isn't just bad luck. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says about 1 in 10 adults aged 65 to 74, and about 1 in 5 adults 75 and older, have lost all their teeth. The two leading causes are cavities and gum disease, and smoking adds to the risk. Among adults 50 and older, the CDC found tooth loss is more common in people with diabetes, heart disease and other chronic conditions.

The CDC's advice is simple: brush twice a day, floss daily, cut back on sugary foods and drinks, and see a dentist every year for a checkup and cleaning, even if you have no natural teeth. For more on staying well, see our healthy aging guide.

What can I do about dry mouth and denture trouble?

The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR) says dry mouth is not a normal part of aging. Medicines are a common cause, especially some drugs for high blood pressure, depression and bladder problems. Dry mouth raises the risk of tooth decay and fungal infections. It can also make dentures fit poorly and rub sore spots on your gums or the roof of your mouth.

  • Tell your dentist or doctor. They can look for the cause. Don't stop or change a medicine on your own.
  • Sip water often, especially with meals, and try a humidifier at night.
  • Chew sugarless gum or suck on sugarless hard candy to get saliva flowing.
  • Cut back on caffeine, and avoid alcohol and tobacco, which dry out the mouth.
  • Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and use an alcohol-free fluoride rinse.
  • See a dentist promptly for sores, pain, swelling or bleeding gums, and keep up regular visits even if you have no natural teeth.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for dentures?
faq.a: No. Original Medicare doesn't cover dentures, cleanings, fillings or extractions. Some Medicare Advantage plans include dental benefits, so check a plan's benefits summary.

faq.q: Does NJ FamilyCare cover dental care for seniors?
faq.a: Yes. The state's adult dental flyer lists exams, cleanings, X-rays, fillings, extractions, and crowns, root canals and dentures (which may need approval first). Cosmetic work isn't covered.

faq.q: How do I get an appointment at the Rutgers dental school?
faq.a: Call (973) 972-4242 or use the online request form on the school's site for an initial evaluation. There is a fee for that first visit, which includes an exam and X-rays.

faq.q: Is there free dental care for seniors in New Jersey?
faq.a: Dental Lifeline Network's Donated Dental Services program matches people over 65, or with a permanent disability or medically necessary need, who can't afford care with volunteer dentists. Call 973-967-9171 in northern NJ or 732-821-3056 elsewhere.
