title: Medicare open enrollment for 2027: what NJ seniors should check
dek: You have until December 7, 2026 to change Medicare plans for next year. Here is what to look for in your plan's notice, how 2027 drug costs work, how PAAD and Senior Gold fit in, and where New Jersey residents get free help.
keyFacts: Open enrollment for 2027 coverage: October 15 to December 7, 2026. Changes start January 1, 2027.
New Jersey has 72 Medicare Advantage plans for 2027, down from 85 in 2026.
2027 Part D out-of-pocket cap: $2,400 on covered drugs. Highest allowed deductible: $700.
Already in Medicare Advantage? You get one more change January 1 to March 31, 2027.
Free, unbiased counseling from NJ SHIP: 1-800-792-8820.
body:
Every fall, people with Medicare get a short window to fix what is not working. For 2027 coverage, that window is October 15 to December 7, 2026. Any change you make takes effect January 1, 2027.

If you do nothing, most plans simply renew. That is fine if your plan still fits. The trouble is that plans change every year, and in New Jersey a good number of them are changing a lot. This guide walks you through what to check, how drug costs work in 2027, how New Jersey's PAAD and Senior Gold programs fit in, and where to get free, unbiased help.

What can I change during open enrollment?

Between October 15 and December 7 you can:

  • Switch from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage plan, or from Medicare Advantage back to Original Medicare.
  • Switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another, with or without drug coverage.
  • Join, drop or switch a stand-alone Part D drug plan if you have Original Medicare.

The plan must receive your request by December 7. If you make more than one change, the last one you make before the deadline is the one that counts.

WindowDatesWho can use it
Medicare Open EnrollmentOctober 15 to December 7, 2026Everyone with Medicare
Coverage startsJanuary 1, 2027Anyone who made a change
Medicare Advantage Open EnrollmentJanuary 1 to March 31, 2027Only people already in a Medicare Advantage plan

The second chance in January. If you are in a Medicare Advantage plan on January 1, you get one more change between January 1 and March 31. You can switch to a different Advantage plan, or drop Advantage and go back to Original Medicare and add a drug plan. The new coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets your request. People in Original Medicare cannot use this window to switch drug plans.

What changed in my plan for 2027?

Your plan should have mailed you an Annual Notice of Change in September. It lists what is different in January: the premium, deductible, copays, the drug list (called a formulary) and sometimes the network of doctors and hospitals. If you never got it, call the plan and ask for a copy.

This year it deserves a careful read. According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), New Jersey has 72 Medicare Advantage plans for 2027, down from 85 in 2026. The average monthly Advantage premium in New Jersey fell from $23.37 to $20.09, and everyone with Medicare in the state can choose at least one $0 premium plan. A lower premium does not tell you what you will pay at the doctor, though.

Open your notice and look for these five things:

  1. Is the plan still offered in my county? If it is ending, call SHIP right away. You may have extra time and extra rights to choose new coverage.
  2. Did the monthly premium change?
  3. Are my drugs still on the list, and at what tier? A drug moving to a higher tier can cost you hundreds more over a year.
  4. Are my doctors, hospital and pharmacy still in network? Call each office and ask about 2027 specifically.
  5. Did copays for specialists, scans, therapy or hospital stays go up?
A note on Part B for 2027

The 2026 Part B premium is $202.90 a month with a $283 deductible. As of October 30, 2026, CMS had not yet announced the 2027 Part B premium and deductible. We will update this guide when it does. You pay Part B no matter which plan you choose, so it does not change which plan is cheaper.

How do drug costs work in 2027?

The Part D rules got simpler in recent years, and 2027 keeps that shape with higher numbers. These limits apply to stand-alone drug plans and to Medicare Advantage plans that include drug coverage.

Part D rule20262027
Highest deductible a plan may charge$615$700
Yearly cap on your out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs$2,100$2,400

After any deductible, you generally pay 25% of the cost of covered drugs. Once your out-of-pocket spending reaches $2,400 in 2027, you pay nothing more for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the year. Some plans have no deductible at all.

In New Jersey, 11 stand-alone drug plans are available for 2027, and the lowest premium is $5.30 a month, according to CMS. The cheapest premium is often not the cheapest plan once you add up your drugs. Enter every prescription on Medicare.gov and compare the estimated yearly total.

If big bills early in the year are hard on your budget, ask your plan about the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan. It spreads your drug costs into monthly payments across the year. It does not lower what you owe in total.

Extra Help

Extra Help is a federal program that lowers Part D premiums, deductibles and copays for people with limited income and savings. You qualify automatically if you have Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program or Supplemental Security Income (SSI). Others can apply through Social Security online or at 1-800-772-1213. People with Extra Help also do not pay a Part D late enrollment penalty.

PAAD and Senior Gold

New Jersey's two state drug programs work alongside Part D. You still need a Part D plan.

  • PAAD (Pharmaceutical Assistance to the Aged and Disabled) is for 2026 income under $54,943 single or $62,390 married. You pay $5 for generics and $7 for brand-name drugs. PAAD pays the monthly premium for certain basic Part D plans priced at or below the regional benchmark. PAAD may not cover the full premium on a plan priced above the benchmark, so ask before you switch. If you are in Medicare Advantage, your plan must include drug coverage, and PAAD contributes up to the benchmark toward the drug part of the premium.
  • Senior Gold is for 2026 income between $54,943 and $64,943 single, or $62,390 and $72,390 married. You pay $15 plus 50% of the remaining cost of each covered drug. You pay your own Part D premium. Once you spend more than $2,000 (single) or $3,000 (married) out of pocket, you pay a flat $15 per prescription.

Before you switch Part D plans, call the PAAD and Senior Gold hotline at 1-800-792-9745 or ask a SHIP counselor which plans keep your state benefit working smoothly. Our guides to PAAD and Senior Gold explain how to apply.

Should I switch between Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage?

This is the biggest decision you can make in the fall, and the hardest one to undo. Our guide to Medicare Advantage or Medigap covers the tradeoffs in depth. Here is what matters most during open enrollment.

Moving from Original Medicare to Medicare Advantage is easy. If you have a Medigap policy, do not cancel it until your Advantage plan is confirmed. If this is your first time in an Advantage plan and you dropped a Medigap policy to join, federal rules give you a 12-month trial period. Return to Original Medicare within that year and you can get your old Medigap policy back if the same company still sells it, or buy certain other policies.

Moving from Medicare Advantage back to Original Medicare is also easy. Getting a Medigap policy afterward may not be. In New Jersey you can apply for Medigap any time of year. Outside your first six months on Part B, and outside a guaranteed issue situation, insurers can ask health questions and may turn you down or charge more. Guaranteed issue situations include your Advantage plan leaving your area. If your plan is ending in 2027, ask SHIP whether you have that right and when to apply.

Before you drop an Advantage plan, get a Medigap answer in writing.

For a county-by-county look at what is available, see Advantage and Medigap by county.

How do I compare plans on Medicare.gov?

  1. Gather your list. Your Medicare card, every prescription with dose and how often you take it, your doctors, your preferred pharmacy and your current plan's Annual Notice of Change.
  2. Go to the Plan Finder. Visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare. Logging in lets you see your current plan and save your drugs and doctors.
  3. Enter your ZIP code and drugs. Pick your pharmacy. Prices can differ between pharmacies, and mail order can be cheaper.
  4. Sort by total estimated yearly cost, which adds premiums and drug costs together.
  5. Check doctors and star ratings. The Plan Finder lets you save providers, but always confirm by calling each office.
  6. Enroll. Use the Enroll button, call the plan directly, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), which is open 24 hours a day.

Rather have a person sit with you? New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) has trained volunteer counselors in all 21 counties. They do not sell insurance or recommend a company. Call 1-800-792-8820 or your county office on aging. Call early in the season so you are not rushed.

How do I spot an enrollment scam?

Scammers know the calendar too. Medicare will never call you out of the blue to sell you a plan, visit your home, or ask for your Medicare number, Social Security number or bank details. Medicare cards are free and come in the mail automatically.

  • Hang up on cold calls that claim to be from Medicare, even if caller ID says Medicare. Caller ID can be faked.
  • Do not join a plan over the phone unless you placed the call.
  • Be wary of TV ads that promise extra cash or "benefits you are missing." They usually connect you to a sales agent.
  • Read your Medicare statements for services or equipment you never received.

Report suspected fraud to 1-800-MEDICARE or to New Jersey's Senior Medicare Patrol at 1-732-777-1940, ext. 1117. For more on common cons, see our scams guide.

Your checklist before December 7

  • Read your Annual Notice of Change. Note any premium, copay, drug or network changes.
  • Confirm your plan is still offered in your county for 2027.
  • Make a list of every prescription, with dose.
  • Call your doctors and ask, "Will you be in network with my plan in 2027?"
  • Compare at least three plans on Medicare.gov by total yearly cost.
  • If you have PAAD or Senior Gold, check how a new Part D plan affects your benefit.
  • If money is tight, apply for Extra Help and a Medicare Savings Program through NJ Save.
  • Thinking of leaving Medicare Advantage? Check your Medigap options first.
  • Book a free SHIP appointment at 1-800-792-8820 if you want help.
  • Keep your confirmation number and watch for a letter from your new plan.

Mark key dates on your calendar, and if you are still under 65, start with Medicare 101.

faq.q: When is Medicare open enrollment for 2027 in New Jersey?
faq.a: October 15 to December 7, 2026. The plan must receive your request by December 7, and the new coverage starts January 1, 2027.

faq.q: What is the Part D out-of-pocket limit for 2027?
faq.a: $2,400 for covered Part D drugs, up from $2,100 in 2026. Once you reach it, you pay nothing more for covered drugs for the rest of 2027. Plans may charge a deductible of up to $700.

faq.q: Do I have to do anything if I want to keep my plan?
faq.a: No. If your plan is still offered, it renews on its own. Read your Annual Notice of Change first to make sure the costs, drug list and doctors still work for you.

faq.q: Can I switch from Medicare Advantage to Original Medicare and get a Medigap policy?
faq.a: You can switch during open enrollment or from January 1 to March 31. In New Jersey, insurers can ask health questions for Medigap outside your first six months on Part B unless you have a guaranteed issue right, so check your Medigap options before you leave the Advantage plan.

faq.q: Do I still need a Part D plan if I have PAAD or Senior Gold?
faq.a: Yes. Both programs require Medicare-eligible members to enroll in Part D. PAAD pays the premium for certain basic plans at or below the regional benchmark, while Senior Gold members pay their own premium.

faq.q: Where can I get free help choosing a Medicare plan in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820 or your county office on aging. SHIP counselors do not sell insurance. You can also call 1-800-MEDICARE any time.

title: Preventing falls at home for seniors in New Jersey
dek: A home safety checklist, free balance classes through New Jersey's county offices on aging, what to ask your doctor, what to do after a fall and who can help pay for grab bars or a ramp.
keyFacts: More than 1 in 4 adults 65 and older falls each year, and fewer than half tell their doctor (CDC).
A Matter of Balance runs eight two-hour sessions for adults 60 and older in selected NJ counties.
Original Medicare does not pay for medical alert systems. Some Advantage plans, MLTSS and JACC may.
JACC can pay for home modifications for people 60+ who need nursing home level care but are not on Medicaid.
Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging.
body:
Most falls do not come out of nowhere. They usually build from a few small things at once: weaker legs, a new pill, old glasses, a loose rug in a dim hallway. Fix two or three of those and the odds change.

This guide covers what actually lowers fall risk for older adults in New Jersey. It walks through a home checklist, the free and low-cost balance classes run through the state and county offices on aging, the questions to ask a doctor and pharmacist, what to do after a fall, and where to get help paying for grab bars or a ramp.

How common are falls, and why do they matter so much?

Falls are the leading cause of injury for adults 65 and older, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). More than one in four older adults falls each year, which is over 14 million people. Fewer than half tell their doctor. Falling once doubles the chance of falling again.

The CDC also reports that the fall death rate among older adults rose 21% between 2018 and 2024. Each year there are about 4.5 million emergency room visits for falls in this age group, and nearly 319,000 older people are hospitalized for hip fractures. Most hip fractures are caused by falls, and many people never return to living on their own after one.

Fear matters too. People who are afraid of falling often move less. Then their legs get weaker, and their risk goes up. The goal is to stay active and get safer at the same time.

One fall is a warning. Treat it as a reason to act, even if nobody got hurt.

What should I fix at home first?

The CDC's STEADI program (Stopping Elderly Accidents, Deaths and Injuries) publishes a free home checklist called Check for Safety. New Jersey's Division of Aging Services also shares an "18 Steps to Fall Proofing Your Home" sheet on its falls prevention page. Walk through the house with one of them. Here is a short version.

Floors and stairs

  • Remove throw rugs, or tape them down firmly.
  • Clear shoes, papers, cords and clutter from walkways.
  • Fix broken or uneven steps, inside and out.
  • Put sturdy railings on both sides of every staircase, including the short half flights in split-level homes.
  • Add light switches or bright bulbs at the top and bottom of stairs.

Bathroom

  • Install grab bars inside and outside the tub or shower and next to the toilet. A towel bar will not hold body weight.
  • Use a nonslip mat or strips in the tub.
  • Consider a shower chair, a handheld shower head and a raised toilet seat.

Bedroom, kitchen and entries

  • Keep a lamp within reach of the bed and night lights on the path to the bathroom.
  • Move everyday dishes and food to shelves between waist and shoulder height so nobody climbs on a step stool.
  • Light every outside door, and line up help with snow and ice before the first storm. Our winter guide has ideas.

Many of these fixes cost little. For a room by room plan with prices, see our aging in place guide.

Where can I take a balance or fall prevention class in New Jersey?

Exercise that builds leg strength and balance is one of the best ways to prevent falls. The CDC names tai chi as a good example. New Jersey's Division of Aging Services supports several proven programs through county offices on aging, senior centers, libraries and senior housing. Availability changes by county and season, so call before you go.

A Matter of Balance

This program, developed from research at Boston University, is for people who worry about falling. Groups of 10 to 12 meet for eight two-hour sessions. You learn to see falls as preventable, set goals for staying active, make your home safer and do exercises for strength and balance. It is designed for adults 60 and older who are mobile and living in the community. The state says it runs in selected counties. The Division of Aging Services 2026 Program Guide lists 609-564-2617 for help finding a class.

Tai chi

The state's falls prevention materials promote Tai Ji Quan: Moving for Better Balance. Many senior centers also offer tai chi. For example, Somerset County's six Senior Wellness Centers list tai chi among their classes for county residents 60 and older. Call the Somerset County Office on Aging and Disability Services at 908-704-6346. In other counties, ask your county office on aging what runs near you.

Other state-supported programs

  • Otago Exercise Program. A physical therapist visits at home four times over two months, with a booster at six months. The state says it is very limited in New Jersey, so ask early.
  • Move Today. A 30 to 45 minute class for flexibility, balance and stamina, done seated or standing, with a strong focus on posture and falls.
  • Project Healthy Bones. A 24-week exercise and education program for people with or at risk of osteoporosis.

To find classes in your county, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737. The state's free GetSetUp site also has live online classes for New Jerseyans 60 and older.

What should I ask my doctor and pharmacist?

Tell your doctor about every fall or near fall since your last visit, even if you were not hurt. A fall can point to a new health problem or a medicine that needs to change. Then ask these questions.

  • Can you check my fall risk? Doctors who use STEADI may test how you walk, stand up from a chair and keep your balance.
  • Could any of my medicines make me dizzy or sleepy? Bring every bottle, including vitamins and over the counter sleep aids. The CDC lists tranquilizers, sedatives and antidepressants among medicines that can affect balance. Never stop a medicine on your own.
  • Should my blood pressure be checked lying down and standing? Blood pressure that drops when you stand up can make you wobbly.
  • Should I take vitamin D, and should I be screened for osteoporosis?
  • Would physical therapy help? Medicare Part B covers medically necessary outpatient physical therapy when your provider certifies it. After the Part B deductible you usually pay 20%.

Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a review of your current prescriptions and a written prevention plan. It is a good time to bring up falls. Our healthy aging guide explains what the visit covers.

Vision and footwear

The CDC recommends an eye exam at least once a year and updating glasses when needed. Bifocal and progressive lenses can make steps look closer or farther than they are. Some people keep a pair with only their distance prescription for walking outside.

Shoes matter more than most people think. The National Institute on Aging suggests nonskid, rubber-soled, low-heeled shoes that fully support the foot. Avoid walking on stairs or bare floors in socks, backless slippers or smooth-soled shoes. If your feet hurt, see a podiatrist. Foot pain changes how you walk.

What should you do after a fall?

If you fall, the National Institute on Aging suggests these steps.

  1. Stay still and breathe. Take a few deep breaths and get over the shock before you move.
  2. Decide if you are hurt. Getting up too fast, or the wrong way, can make an injury worse.
  3. Roll to your side and rest. If you think you can get up safely, roll over, rest, then get on your hands and knees.
  4. Crawl to a sturdy chair. Put your hands on the seat, bring one foot forward flat on the floor and slowly rise and turn to sit.
  5. Get help if you need it. If you are hurt or cannot get up, call 911 or someone nearby. If you are alone, get as comfortable as you can and keep warm while you wait.
Hit your head?

The CDC says an older adult who falls and hits their head should see a doctor right away to check for a brain injury. This matters even more for anyone taking a blood thinner.

After any fall, make an appointment with the doctor. Write down what happened, where, what time and what you were doing. That helps the doctor find the cause.

Medical alert options

Keep a charged cell phone on you, and set up a daily check-in call with family or a friend. A personal emergency response system adds a button worn on the wrist or neck that calls a monitoring center. Some models detect falls automatically, and some smartwatches have a similar feature.

Original Medicare does not pay for medical alert systems. Some Medicare Advantage plans cover part or all of the cost, so check your plan's benefits. In New Jersey, Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) and the state's Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC) program can include a personal emergency response system for people who qualify. Before you sign up for any service, ask about equipment fees, monthly charges, contract length and how to cancel.

Who can help pay for grab bars, railings or a ramp in New Jersey?

Start with one free call to the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. It connects you to your county Area Agency on Aging, also called the county office on aging. The state's 2026 Program Guide lists home repairs among the in-home support services these offices provide or coordinate. What is offered, and how long the wait is, differs by county.

  • JACC. A state-funded program for people 60 and older who need a nursing home level of care but are not on Medicaid. Services can include home modifications, medical equipment and a personal emergency response system. In 2026 the income limit is $4,855 a month for one person or $6,582 for a couple, with countable assets of $40,000 or less for one person or $60,000 for a couple. Services are capped at $1,156 a month plus care management, and a sliding-scale copay may apply. See our JACC guide.
  • MLTSS. New Jersey's Medicaid long-term care benefit can cover home and vehicle modifications and a personal emergency response system for members who qualify. See our MLTSS guide.
  • Veterans. The VA's Home Improvements and Structural Alterations grant can help with medically needed changes like ramps and accessible bathrooms. See our veterans benefits guide.
  • Weatherization. If drafty doors or failing heat are part of the problem, the free Weatherization Assistance Program is requested on the same application as LIHEAP. See our LIHEAP guide.

If you hire a contractor, make sure the company is registered with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs and get a written contract. Our aging in place guide explains how to check.

Who do I call?

NeedWhoNumber

title: Chair yoga for seniors in New Jersey: benefits, safety and classes
dek: What chair yoga is, what the research says, who should check with a doctor first, a gentle routine to try at home, and where to find classes across New Jersey.
keyFacts: Federal health researchers say yoga may improve balance, sleep and stress, and ease some neck and knee pain.
Yoga injuries treated in emergency rooms are more common in people 65 and older, so start with a qualified teacher (NCCIH).
NIA recommends about three sessions of balance exercise a week. Yoga counts.
Move Today, a state supported class, can be done sitting or standing. Help finding a class: 609-564-2617.
Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to find chair yoga at a senior center near you.
body:
Chair yoga gives you the stretching, breathing and balance work of yoga without getting down on the floor, and without worrying about how you will get back up.

This guide explains what chair yoga is, what the research says, who should check with a doctor first and how to try a gentle routine at home. It also lists real places in New Jersey to find a class, many of them free or close to it.

What is chair yoga?

Chair yoga is regular yoga adapted so you can do most of it seated in a sturdy chair. Some poses are done standing, with one hand on the chair back for support. A class usually mixes three things: gentle movement for the neck, shoulders, spine, hips and ankles; slow breathing; and a few quiet minutes of relaxation at the end.

The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), part of the National Institutes of Health, describes yoga as practiced in the United States as physical postures, breathing techniques and meditation. Chair yoga keeps all three. It just moves them off the mat.

It suits a lot of people. Those with stiff knees or hips. People recovering from an illness. Anyone who feels unsteady standing for long. People who used to do yoga and want to keep going. Many classes welcome people who use a walker or a wheelchair, though you should ask first.

If you can sit in a chair and breathe, you can probably do some chair yoga.

What are the benefits, according to the research?

Research on yoga is still growing, and studies use many different styles. Here is what the federal health agencies say, in plain terms.

  • Balance. NCCIH reports that 11 of 15 studies in a 2014 review found improvement in at least one measure of balance, and that newer studies support a benefit for older adults living in the community.
  • Sleep and stress. NCCIH says yoga has been shown to help sleep in several studies, including studies of older adults. Reviews also found benefits for stress and general mental well being.
  • Pain. Yoga may ease neck pain and the pain of knee osteoarthritis, and may help low back pain a little. NCCIH calls the evidence for knee and neck promising but limited.
  • Mood. Yoga may help people manage symptoms of anxiety or depression.

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) lists yoga as a balance exercise and says activities like yoga count as a mix of exercise types. NIA recommends about three sessions of balance exercise a week for older adults. A chair yoga class two or three times a week can cover much of that.

Keep the claims modest. Chair yoga will not replace walking or strength training, and it will not cure arthritis. It is a gentle, social way to move more, and moving more is what the research keeps rewarding.

Is chair yoga safe for me, and when should I ask a doctor first?

For most people, yes. NCCIH says yoga is generally safe for healthy people when done properly with a qualified instructor. It also gives older adults a specific caution: emergency room visits for yoga injuries are more common in people 65 and older than in younger adults. Most injuries are sprains and strains, often in the knee or lower leg.

NCCIH advises older adults and people with health conditions to talk with their health care provider and the instructor about their needs. It lists these among the conditions that may call for changes:

  • An earlier injury, such as a knee or hip injury
  • Lumbar spine disease
  • Severe high blood pressure
  • Balance problems
  • Glaucoma

If you have osteoporosis, a joint replacement or a recent fall, ask your doctor which bends, twists and standing poses are safe for you.

Beginners should skip extreme poses such as headstands, shoulder stands and forceful breathing, and avoid hot yoga. Do not use yoga to put off seeing a doctor about a new symptom. Stop and get help if you feel chest pain or pressure, dizziness or nausea. NIA lists those as warning signs during aerobic exercise.

Choose the right chair

Use a sturdy chair without wheels or arms, set against a wall or on a nonslip rug. Your feet should rest flat on the floor. If they do not reach, put a firm cushion or a thick book under them.

What does a gentle routine look like?

Here is a simple sequence you can try at home in about 15 minutes. Move slowly and never push into pain. Breathe through your nose if that is comfortable, and keep breathing the whole time.

  1. Settle in. Sit toward the front of the chair, feet flat and hip width apart, hands on your thighs. Take five slow breaths, letting the exhale run a little longer than the inhale.
  2. Neck and shoulders. Lower your right ear toward your right shoulder, hold for three breaths, then switch sides. Roll your shoulders back in slow circles five times.
  3. Seated reach. Breathe in and raise both arms as high as is comfortable. Breathe out and lower them. Repeat five times. If your shoulders are stiff, raise your arms only to shoulder height.
  4. Cat and cow. With hands on your knees, breathe in and gently lift your chest. Breathe out and round your back, letting your chin drop. Repeat five times.
  5. Gentle twist. Sit tall. Place your left hand on your right knee and your right hand on the seat behind you. Turn slowly to the right and hold for three breaths. Return to center and switch sides. Keep the twist small if you have osteoporosis or back trouble.
  6. Ankles and feet. Lift one foot slightly and circle the ankle five times each way. Then press the heel down and lift the toes, back and forth. Switch feet.
  7. Standing balance, optional. Stand behind the chair with both hands on its back. Rise slowly onto your toes, then lower. Try ten times. If that feels steady, try lifting one foot an inch off the floor for a few seconds while holding on.
  8. Rest. Sit back, close your eyes if you like, and breathe quietly for two minutes.

NIA also posts free exercise videos, and GetSetUp, the online class site New Jersey offers free to older residents, lists seated fitness classes alongside its technology courses. A live teacher is still the best way to learn good form, especially for the first few weeks.

Should I do it at home or take a class?

Both have a place. NCCIH notes that learning yoga on your own, without supervision, has been linked to more injuries. A class gives you a teacher who can correct your posture and adapt poses to your body. It also gives you a reason to get dressed and see people, which matters a lot on a gray February morning.

Home practice works best once you know the basics. Many people take a weekly class and repeat a short routine at home on two other days.

OptionGood forKeep in mind
Senior center or county classLow cost, social, a teacher who knows older bodiesSchedules change by season. Some fill up.
Public library classFree or low cost, close to homeOften runs as a series with registration
Live online classBad weather, no ride, caring for a spouseThe teacher cannot see you as well. Keep the chair against a wall.
Video at homePractice between classesBest after you have learned the moves in person
Private teacher at homeLimited mobility, specific health needsCosts more. Ask about training and insurance.

When you check out a teacher, ask how long they have taught older adults and what training they have. NCCIH suggests asking about an instructor's training and experience before you start.

Where can I find chair yoga in New Jersey?

County senior centers and offices on aging

Your county office on aging is the best first call. It knows which senior centers, town recreation departments and community groups run chair yoga near you. Reach it through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737, or dial 2-1-1 for NJ 211.

As one example, Somerset County's Senior Wellness Centers listed several chair yoga classes in their winter 2026 schedules. They included a video led class on Monday mornings and an eight week series with an instructor that cost $40. Call the Somerset County Office on Aging and Disability Services at 908-704-6346 for current classes. Most counties have something similar, so ask.

Public libraries

Many New Jersey libraries host chair yoga. The Newark Public Library, for example, began a weekly chair yoga class on Tuesday mornings this fall in the Main Library auditorium, aimed at older adults and people with limited mobility. The library supplies chairs, and registration is encouraged. Check your own library's events calendar, or ask at the desk.

State supported programs

New Jersey's Division of Aging Services supports several proven exercise programs run through county partners. None is called chair yoga, but two are close cousins:

  • Move Today is a 30 to 45 minute class for flexibility, balance and stamina. You can do the exercises sitting or standing, with stretch bands. Trained peer leaders run it weekly or every other week for 12 sessions, with a strong focus on posture and preventing falls.
  • A Matter of Balance runs for eight two-hour sessions and helps people who worry about falling. It is for adults 60 and older who are mobile, and it is offered in selected counties.

The Division's 2026 Program Guide lists 609-564-2617 for help finding these classes. Our fall prevention guide covers both in more detail.

YMCAs and community centers

Many YMCAs and town recreation centers in New Jersey run gentle yoga and chair based fitness classes for older adults. Some Medicare Advantage plans include a fitness benefit that covers a basic membership at participating locations. Original Medicare does not cover gym memberships or fitness programs, so call your plan to check. Our guide to exercise at home explains these benefits.

Online, free for New Jerseyans

The state's partnership with GetSetUp offers free live online classes for New Jersey residents 60 and older, including seated fitness and breathing sessions. If you need help getting online, see our guide to tech help in New Jersey.

How do I get started this week?

  1. Tell your doctor. Mention it at your next visit, or call first if you have any condition on the list above.
  2. Make one call. Ring the ADRC or your library and ask, "Where is the nearest chair yoga class for older adults?"
  3. Go twice before you judge. The first class always feels awkward.
  4. Add ten minutes at home. Repeat a few moves you learned on two other days.

Chair yoga pairs well with walking and simple strength work. For a full weekly plan, read our guide to exercising at home, and for more on staying well, see healthy aging in New Jersey. If getting out is hard, our list of activities for older adults who can't easily leave home has more ideas.

faq.q: Is chair yoga real exercise?
faq.a: Yes. It works flexibility and balance, and some poses build strength. The National Institute on Aging lists yoga as a balance exercise. It does not replace walking or strength training, so pair it with other activity.

faq.q: Do I need a doctor's permission for chair yoga?
faq.a: Most people can start without one, but NCCIH advises older adults and people with health conditions to talk with their provider first. Check in if you have had a joint replacement, back problems, severe high blood pressure, glaucoma, osteoporosis, balance problems or a recent fall.

faq.q: Can I do chair yoga if I use a walker or wheelchair?
faq.a: Often yes, since most of it is done seated. Ask the instructor before your first class so they can adapt the poses for you.

faq.q: How much does a chair yoga class cost in New Jersey?
faq.a: Many library and senior center classes are free or low cost. For example, a Somerset County Senior Wellness Center series in winter 2026 cost $40 for eight weeks. Prices vary, so ask when you register.

faq.q: Where can I find a class near me?
faq.a: Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging, check your public library's events calendar, or ask your town recreation department or local YMCA.

title: Exercise at home for seniors in New Jersey: a safe weekly plan
dek: How much activity older adults need, simple strength, balance and stretching moves for home, a sample week, when to stop, and what Medicare and New Jersey programs cover.
keyFacts: CDC: adults 65+ need 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, 2 days of strength work and balance activities.
Some activity is better than none. Start small and build slowly.
Medicare Part B covers medically necessary outpatient physical therapy. You pay 20% after the deductible.
Original Medicare does not cover gyms. Some Medicare Advantage plans include SilverSneakers or Renew Active.
NJ's Otago program sends a physical therapist to your home, but spots are very limited. Ask at 609-564-2617.
body:
You do not need a gym to get stronger. A sturdy kitchen chair, a wall, a staircase and a pair of comfortable shoes will take most older adults a long way. What you need more is a plan you can stick to.

This guide covers how much activity federal health experts recommend after 65, the four kinds of exercise that matter, a sample week you can do at home, when to stop, and what Medicare and New Jersey programs can help with.

How much exercise do older adults need?

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults 65 and older get, every week:

  • At least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity. That could be 30 minutes a day, five days a week. Or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix of the two.
  • At least 2 days of muscle strengthening that works the legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms.
  • Activities to improve balance, such as walking heel to toe or standing up from a chair.

If that sounds like a lot, the CDC's next line matters most. If you cannot meet the recommendations, be as active as your abilities and conditions allow. Some activity is better than none, and benefits grow the more you do.

How do you know it is moderate? The National Institute on Aging (NIA) suggests a talk test. If you are breathing hard but can still hold a conversation, that is moderate. If you can only say a few words before taking a breath, that is vigorous.

Short bouts of activity count. So do vacuuming, raking and climbing stairs.

What kinds of exercise should I do at home?

NIA groups exercise for older adults into aerobic, muscle strengthening and balance, and adds flexibility as a fourth. NIA says getting all of them matters, and variety helps lower the chance of injury.

Aerobic (endurance)

Anything that gets your heart and breathing up for a while. At home that can mean marching in place, walking laps of the house or apartment hallway, dancing to music, climbing stairs or following an exercise video. NIA counts housework such as mopping and vacuuming, and yard work such as raking, as moderate activity too.

Strength

Strong legs make it easier to get out of a chair, climb stairs and carry groceries, and they help prevent falls. NIA suggests one set of 8 to 12 repetitions of each exercise, done until another repetition would be hard. Two or three sets may work better once you are ready. Rest a muscle group for a day between sessions. Good home moves include:

  • Sit to stand from a chair, using your hands only if you need to
  • Wall pushups
  • Heel raises while holding the back of a chair
  • Side leg raises while holding a chair
  • Arm curls and overhead presses with light hand weights or water bottles
  • Rows with a resistance band looped around a sturdy object

If you are new to this, NIA suggests starting without weights or bands until the movements feel comfortable. Breathe out during the effort and in as you relax. Do not hold your breath, and do not lock your elbows or knees.

Balance

NIA recommends about three sessions of balance exercise a week. Try standing on one foot while holding a chair, the heel to toe walk along a counter, walking sideways or backward with support nearby, and standing up from a chair without using your hands. Tai chi and yoga count too. Our chair yoga guide has a gentle routine.

Flexibility

Stretch after you are warmed up, ideally after walking or strength work. Breathe, and do not stretch so far that it hurts. Flexibility makes daily tasks easier, such as tying shoes or unloading the dishwasher.

What does a sample week look like?

Here is one way to meet the guidelines at home. Adjust it to your energy and health. If you are just starting, cut every number in half for the first two weeks.

DayPlan
Monday30 minutes of walking, inside or out. 10 minutes of stretching.
TuesdayStrength: sit to stand, wall pushups, heel raises, band rows, arm curls. One set of each. Balance practice for 10 minutes.
Wednesday30 minutes of walking, dancing or a video class.
ThursdayBalance and flexibility: chair yoga or tai chi for 20 to 30 minutes.
FridayStrength again, same moves. Balance practice for 10 minutes.
Saturday30 minutes of something you enjoy: a long walk, gardening, a class with a friend.
Sunday30 minutes of walking, or rest if you need it.

That adds up to about 150 minutes of aerobic activity, two strength days and at least three balance sessions. Write each session on a calendar. A check mark is a surprisingly good motivator.

How do I progress safely?

Go slowly. Add five minutes to a walk, or two repetitions to a strength exercise, once the current amount feels easy for a week. NIA says gradual increases in weight, sets, repetitions or days are what make muscles stronger. Never add more than one change at a time.

What equipment helps?

  • A sturdy armless chair without wheels
  • Supportive shoes with nonskid soles
  • A set of resistance bands in a few strengths
  • Light hand weights, or water bottles to start
  • A nonslip mat if you do floor work
  • A water bottle. NIA reminds people to drink water when they sweat, unless a doctor has told them to limit fluids.

Clear a space with no throw rugs or cords. Keep a phone within reach in case you need help.

When should I stop, and who should check with a doctor first?

NIA says aerobic activity should not cause dizziness, chest pain or pressure, or nausea. If any of those happen, stop. For chest pain or pressure that does not go away, call 911.

Also ease off if you feel unsteady, if a joint swells or if pain lingers into the next day. NIA advises people with chronic pain to avoid overdoing it on good days and to rest an area that is painful, swollen or inflamed.

Talk with your doctor before starting if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, COPD, osteoporosis, a recent surgery or fall, or any symptom that worries you. NIA says most older adults with chronic conditions can exercise and benefit from it, but the plan may need adjusting. People with diabetes need to watch blood sugar and protect their feet. People with high blood pressure may need medication changes as they get more active.

After a fall or a hospital stay

Ask your doctor whether physical therapy would help before you start a home program. A therapist can build a plan around your body and show you how to do each move safely.

What does Medicare cover?

Physical therapy

Medicare Part B helps pay for medically necessary outpatient physical therapy when your doctor or another provider, such as a nurse practitioner or physician assistant, certifies that you need it. After the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. There is no yearly dollar limit on medically necessary therapy. Medicare says therapy can also help you keep your current abilities or slow a decline.

If you are homebound, Medicare's home health benefit can cover physical therapy at home when a doctor orders it and a Medicare-certified home health agency provides it. You pay nothing for covered home health services. See our hospital discharge guide for how this works after a hospital stay.

Gym and fitness benefits

Original Medicare does not cover gym memberships or fitness programs. Some Medicare Advantage plans, and some Medigap policies, include them as an extra.

  • SilverSneakers is included with many Medicare Advantage plans at no added cost. Members get live online classes, on demand workout videos and a basic membership at participating gyms and community centers. Classes include chair and standing yoga and many seated workouts. You can check eligibility with the program at 866-584-7389.
  • Renew Active is a fitness program offered with some Medicare Advantage plans and some Medicare Supplement plans. It includes a gym membership at network locations, on demand workout videos and live streaming classes.

Benefits vary by plan and county, so call the number on your plan card. During Medicare open enrollment, which runs October 15 to December 7, you can compare plans with free help from New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820. Our open enrollment guide explains how to compare.

Which New Jersey programs can help me exercise safely?

The New Jersey Division of Aging Services supports several proven exercise programs through county offices on aging, health departments and community groups. They are free or low cost, but availability changes by county and season.

  • A Matter of Balance. Eight two-hour sessions for groups of 10 to 12, for adults 60 and older who worry about falling. It includes exercise for strength and balance. Offered in selected counties.
  • Move Today. A 30 to 45 minute class for flexibility, balance and stamina, done sitting or standing with stretch bands. Trained peer leaders run 12 sessions.
  • The Otago Exercise Program. This one comes to you. A physical therapist, sometimes with an assistant or nurse, visits four times at home over two months and again at six months, with monthly phone check-ins in between. You do strength and balance exercises 30 minutes three times a week and walk twice a week when appropriate. The state says Otago has reduced falls and related injury risk by 35% and is meant for people who cannot or do not want to attend a group class. It is very limited in New Jersey, so ask early.
  • Project Healthy Bones. A 24-week exercise and education program for people with or at risk of osteoporosis.

For any of these, the Division's 2026 Program Guide lists 609-564-2617. You can also call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging, which knows about local senior center classes too.

If you would rather exercise online, New Jersey offers free live classes through GetSetUp for residents 60 and older, including seated workouts. Our tech help guide explains where to get help joining.

Exercise is one of the best things you can do to prevent falls. For a home safety checklist and what to do after a fall, read our fall prevention guide.

faq.q: How many minutes of exercise do older adults need each week?
faq.a: The CDC recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, such as 30 minutes on five days, plus at least two days of muscle strengthening and activities to improve balance. If you cannot reach that, do as much as your health allows.

faq.q: Can I build strength without weights?
faq.a: Yes. Sit to stand from a chair, wall pushups and heel raises use your own body weight. NIA suggests beginners start without weights or bands until the movements feel comfortable.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a gym membership?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not. Some Medicare Advantage plans and some Medigap policies include fitness programs such as SilverSneakers or Renew Active. Call your plan to check, or get free help comparing plans from SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

faq.q: Will Medicare pay for physical therapy at home?
faq.a: If you are homebound and a doctor orders it, Medicare's home health benefit can cover physical therapy at home through a Medicare-certified agency. Outpatient therapy is covered under Part B when a provider certifies you need it.

faq.q: When should I stop exercising?
faq.a: Stop if you feel dizzy, have chest pain or pressure, or feel sick to your stomach. Call 911 for chest pain or pressure that does not go away. Ease off if a joint swells or you feel unsteady, and talk with your doctor.
